# Overview

## What the Environment Factory is

Every E2E test needs data. A test for "user adds item to cart" needs a user, products, and a cart. A test for "admin views analytics" needs an organization with users, runs, and history.

Tests can't share data -- if one test deletes a product, another test that expects 10 products will fail. When tests run in parallel, this gets worse.

The Environment Factory solves this. It's a single POST endpoint in your backend that the Autonoma platform calls to:

1. Create fresh, isolated data before each test run
2. Tear down that data after the test finishes

Each test run gets its own organization, users, and data. No interference between tests.

## What the SDK does

The Autonoma SDK is a set of packages that you install in your backend. Together they implement the entire Environment Factory endpoint. You configure it with your database connection, a scope field, two secrets, and an auth callback.

The SDK handles everything:
- Reading your database schema (models and fields) via discover
- Creating records through your registered factories, ordered from the `_alias`/`_ref` graph in the create payload
- Tearing down all created data without leaving orphans
- Verifying incoming request signatures (HMAC-SHA256)
- Signing teardown tokens so nobody can tamper with them
- Gating the endpoint behind an explicit allowProduction flag (no NODE_ENV guessing)

You write minimal configuration code. The SDK does the rest.

SDKs are available for TypeScript, Python, and Elixir. Each language provides a core protocol library, ORM adapters (for your database layer), and server/framework adapters (for your HTTP framework). You install one of each.

## The three actions

The endpoint handles three actions via POST:

discover -- The platform asks "what does your database look like?" The SDK reads your ORM schema and returns the models and their fields (plus the scope field name). It does NOT introspect FK relations — the `edges` and `relations` arrays are emitted empty. The platform uses the model/field info to generate valid scenario data.

up -- The platform sends scenario data: a flat map keyed by model name, where each value is an array of records to create. Cross-model links are expressed with `_alias`/`_ref`. The SDK topologically sorts the records from that `_alias`/`_ref` graph, creates each through its registered factory, and returns auth credentials so the test runner can log in. It also returns a signed token for teardown.

down -- The platform sends the signed token back. The SDK verifies it and deletes everything that was created -- in the correct order, without FK constraint violations.

## What you provide

adapter       Your ORM adapter configured with a scope field.
sharedSecret  A secret shared between you and Autonoma -- verifies incoming requests.
signingSecret A secret only you know -- signs the teardown token so nobody can tamper with it.
auth          A callback that creates real login credentials for test users.

## The scope field

Most multi-tenant apps have a foreign key like organizationId on every model. This is the "scope field" -- it's how the SDK isolates test data.

During creation: the SDK does NOT inject the scope field. You set it explicitly on every model that has it -- normally as a `{ "_ref": "..." }` pointing at the scope record. The registered factory owns the actual write. The scope field is read only AFTER create, to derive the auth scope value for the response.

During teardown: the SDK deletes everything where the scope field equals the test organization's ID, in reverse topological order (derived from the payload's `_alias`/`_ref` graph) to avoid constraint violations.

Example: if your database has Organization, User, and Application models, and both User and Application have an organizationId column pointing to Organization, then organizationId is your scope field. You write a flat create payload:
1. Organization with an `_alias` (e.g. "org")
2. Users and Applications, each with `organizationId` set to `{ "_ref": "org" }`
3. The SDK orders the records from the `_ref` graph, creates the Organization first, then the Users and Applications via their factories. On teardown, it deletes Applications, then Users, then the Organization.

If your app isn't multi-tenant, you'll need a dedicated field (like testRunId) on every model.

Limitation: The scope field must be a single column. Compound scope keys (e.g., organizationId + countryId) are not supported. If your app scopes by multiple fields, use a single root entity with its own ID that child models reference.

## The two secrets

You need two different secrets. The SDK will throw an error if they are the same.

Shared secret (AUTONOMA_SHARED_SECRET): Both you and Autonoma know this. Autonoma signs every request with HMAC-SHA256; your endpoint verifies the signature. This prevents unauthorized calls to your endpoint.

Signing secret (AUTONOMA_SIGNING_SECRET): Only you know this. During up, the SDK signs a token containing the IDs of all created records. During down, it verifies the token before deleting. Even Autonoma can't forge or modify this token -- they just store it and pass it back.

Generate both with different values:

  openssl rand -hex 32   # use as AUTONOMA_SHARED_SECRET
  openssl rand -hex 32   # use as AUTONOMA_SIGNING_SECRET (must be different!)

## Handling updates

The platform sends scenario data inline in the up request. If your schema changes (you add a model, rename a field), the platform sees the change on the next discover call. There are no local files to keep in sync.

## SDK availability

SDKs are available for three languages:

TypeScript -- ORM adapters for Prisma and Drizzle. Server adapters for Web standard (Next.js, Hono, Bun, Deno), Express, and Node.js http.

Python -- ORM adapters for SQLAlchemy and other Python ORMs. Server adapters for popular Python web frameworks.

Elixir -- ORM adapters for Ecto. Server adapters for Phoenix and Plug.

Each language follows the same architecture: a core protocol library plus ORM and server adapter packages. The protocol behavior is identical across languages -- only the package names and syntax differ.

See the language-specific documentation in each SDK directory for installation instructions and code examples.


---

# Autonoma Environment Factory Protocol

## Overview

The Environment Factory protocol defines how the Autonoma platform communicates with your backend to create and destroy isolated test data. It is a simple request-response protocol over HTTP POST with HMAC-SHA256 authentication.

Protocol version: 1.0

## Transport

All communication happens over a single HTTP POST endpoint. The URL is chosen by you (e.g., /api/autonoma). The platform sends JSON requests and expects JSON responses.

## Authentication

Every request is authenticated with HMAC-SHA256. The platform computes the signature over the raw request body using the shared secret and includes it in the x-signature header.

The SDK verifies the signature before processing any request. If the signature is missing or invalid, the request is rejected with a 401 status.

### The two secrets

The protocol uses two separate secrets. They must be different values.

Shared secret: Known by both the Autonoma platform and your backend. Used for HMAC-SHA256 request signing. The platform signs; your SDK verifies.

Signing secret: Known only by your backend. Used to sign the refs token during up and verify it during down. The platform stores this token opaquely and passes it back -- it cannot read or modify it.

## Request format

Every request is an HTTP POST with:
- Content-Type: application/json
- x-signature: HMAC-SHA256 hex digest of the raw body, keyed with the shared secret

The request body is a JSON object with an "action" field that determines the operation.

## Response format

Every response is a JSON object. Successful responses include metadata fields:

  version   The protocol version string (currently "1.0").
  sdk       An object with language, orm, and server fields identifying the SDK implementation.

Error responses include:

  error     A human-readable error message.
  code      A machine-readable error code string.

## Actions

### discover

Request:

  {
    "action": "discover"
  }

Response (200):

  {
    "version": "1.0",
    "sdk": { "language": "typescript", "orm": "prisma", "server": "web" },
    "schema": {
      "models": [ ... ],
      "edges": [],
      "relations": [],
      "scopeField": "organizationId"
    }
  }

The schema object contains:
- models: list of all database models with their fields (name, type, isRequired, isId, hasDefault). This and scopeField are the meaningful parts.
- edges: always emitted as an empty array. The SDK does NOT introspect FK relations.
- relations: always emitted as an empty array. The SDK does NOT introspect FK relations.
- scopeField: the field name used for test data isolation

Dependency information does not come from the schema. The SDK derives create order entirely from the `_alias`/`_ref` graph in the up payload at request time.

### up

Request:

  {
    "action": "up",
    "testRunId": "optional-uuid",
    "create": {
      "Organization": [{ "_alias": "org", "name": "Acme Corp", "slug": "acme-corp" }],
      "User": [{ "_alias": "alice", "email": "alice@test.com", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } }],
      "Member": [{ "role": "owner", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" }, "userId": { "_ref": "alice" } }]
    }
  }

If testRunId is omitted, the SDK generates a random UUID.

The create field is a FLAT map keyed by model name; each value is an array of records to create. A model is created only when it appears as a top-level key. There is no nesting — cross-model links are expressed with `_alias`/`_ref`. See scenarios.txt for the full format.

Response (200):

  {
    "version": "1.0",
    "sdk": { "language": "typescript", "orm": "prisma", "server": "web" },
    "auth": { "token": "...", "cookies": [...], "credentials": {...} },
    "refs": {
      "ModelName": [{ "id": "...", "field": "value", ... }]
    },
    "refsToken": "header.payload.signature"
  }

- auth: credentials for the test runner to authenticate (format depends on auth callback)
- refs: all created records, keyed by model name
- refsToken: a signed token encoding the created record IDs, used for teardown

### down

Request:

  {
    "action": "down",
    "refsToken": "header.payload.signature"
  }

The refsToken is the exact token returned by the up response.

Response (200):

  {
    "version": "1.0",
    "sdk": { "language": "typescript", "orm": "prisma", "server": "web" },
    "ok": true
  }

## The scope field

The scope field is a single column name (e.g., organizationId) present on most models in the database. It references a root entity (e.g., Organization) that acts as the isolation boundary for test data.

During up: the SDK does NOT inject the scope field. Every model that has the scope field must set it explicitly in the payload — normally as a `{ "_ref": "..." }` to the scope record — and the registered factory writes it. The SDK reads the scope field only AFTER create, to derive the auth scope value for the response.

During teardown: the SDK does not use the scope field to find rows. It tears down exactly the records captured in the signed refs token, calling each model's factory `teardown` per record in reverse topological order (derived from the up payload's `_alias`/`_ref` graph) to respect FK constraints. A model whose factory defines no `teardown` is skipped.

## The refs token

The refs token is a JWT-like structure (header.payload.signature) signed with the signing secret. It contains:
- The test run ID (scope value)
- All created record IDs, keyed by model name

The token is signed by the SDK during up and verified during down. Because only your backend knows the signing secret, the token cannot be forged or modified by the platform or any external party. This ensures that down can only delete records that up created.

## Safety model

The protocol enforces hard safety constraints:

1. EXPLICIT OPT-IN
   The endpoint returns 404 PRODUCTION_BLOCKED unless allowProduction is set to true. The SDK does not inspect NODE_ENV (or any environment variable) — this explicit flag is the only switch. This keeps the gate explicit and visible instead of relying on implicit environment detection.

2. UP CAN ONLY CREATE
   The up action routes every record through a registered factory's create. The SDK itself never updates, deletes, drops, truncates, or runs SQL. The worst it can do is insert rows.

3. DOWN CAN ONLY DELETE WHAT UP CREATED
   During up, the SDK signs a token with the IDs of every created record using your signing secret. During down, the SDK verifies that token before deleting. It deletes only the records listed in the token. Even the Autonoma platform cannot forge or modify this token.

4. REQUESTS ARE AUTHENTICATED
   Every request is HMAC-SHA256 signed with the shared secret. Unsigned or tampered requests are rejected with 401.

5. FACTORY-DRIVEN WRITES
   Every model the SDK writes goes through a registered factory's create — the SDK never runs SQL itself and never falls back to it. (A factory body may do a raw INSERT internally; that is owned by you, not the SDK.)

## Error codes

  Code                  HTTP Status  Meaning
  INVALID_SIGNATURE     401          HMAC signature missing or does not match
  INVALID_BODY          400          Request body is not valid JSON, or missing required fields
  UNKNOWN_ACTION        400          The action field is not discover, up, or down
  UNKNOWN_ENVIRONMENT   400          The requested environment name does not exist
  INVALID_REFS_TOKEN    403          The refs token is missing, malformed, or signature verification failed
  PRODUCTION_BLOCKED    404          Endpoint is disabled — allowProduction is not set to true
  SAME_SECRETS          500          sharedSecret and signingSecret are the same value
  INTERNAL_ERROR        500          Unexpected server error

## HMAC signature computation

The signature is computed as:

  HMAC-SHA256(raw_request_body_bytes, shared_secret) -> hex digest

The platform sends this as the x-signature header value. The SDK recomputes the HMAC over the raw body string (before JSON parsing) and compares using a constant-time comparison.

Important: the signature is computed over the exact bytes of the request body. The server adapter must extract the raw body as a string before any JSON parsing or middleware transformation.


---

# Writing Scenario Data

Scenario data describes what database records to create. The Autonoma platform generates this from your schema, but you may write it for integration tests and debugging.

## Why not raw SQL?

The Environment Factory is designed with hard constraints that make it safe by construction:

1. EXPLICIT OPT-IN
   The endpoint returns 404 unless allowProduction is set to true. The SDK does not inspect the environment (NODE_ENV, etc.) — this explicit flag is the only switch.

2. UP CAN ONLY CREATE
   The up action routes every record through a registered factory's create. The SDK itself never UPDATEs, DELETEs, DROPs, TRUNCATEs, or runs SQL. The worst it can do is INSERT rows.

3. DOWN CAN ONLY DELETE WHAT UP CREATED
   During up, the SDK signs a token with the IDs of every created record, using your signing secret (not the shared secret). During down, the SDK verifies that token before deleting. It deletes only the records listed in the token. Even Autonoma cannot forge or modify this token.

4. REQUESTS ARE AUTHENTICATED
   Every request is HMAC-SHA256 signed with the shared secret. Unsigned or tampered requests are rejected with 401.

5. FACTORY-DRIVEN WRITES
   Every model the SDK writes goes through a registered factory's create -- the SDK never runs SQL itself and never falls back to it. (A factory body may do a raw INSERT internally; that is owned by you, not the SDK.)

Contrast with raw SQL: a raw SQL endpoint could DROP TABLE, DELETE FROM users, or UPDATE users SET role = 'admin'. Even with auth, one malformed query could destroy production data. The Environment Factory can't do any of that.

This is why scenario data is a structured JSON object, not SQL. The SDK interprets it as a series of factory create calls -- nothing more.

## The format

Data is a FLAT map. The top-level keys are model names from your database schema; each value is an array of records to create for that model. A model is created ONLY when it appears as a top-level key. There is NO nesting -- you do not place one model's records inside another model's fields. (If you do, the SDK treats that array as opaque field data and passes it to the factory verbatim; it is NOT created as separate records.)

Every cross-model link is expressed with `_alias`/`_ref`: name a record with `_alias`, and point a foreign key at it with `{ "_ref": "alias" }`. The SDK topologically sorts the records from this `_alias`/`_ref` graph, so the order of keys does not matter. There is no relation introspection — dependency order comes entirely from the `_ref` edges you write.

All field values must be complete and literal -- the SDK does not perform any template resolution or variable substitution. The platform is responsible for generating fully resolved data before sending it.

### Minimal example (org + user)

  {
    "create": {
      "Organization": [{ "_alias": "org", "name": "Test Org", "slug": "test-org" }],
      "User": [{ "_alias": "admin", "name": "Admin", "email": "admin@test.com", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } }],
      "Member": [{ "role": "owner", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" }, "userId": { "_ref": "admin" } }]
    }
  }

This creates:
1. One Organization (aliased "org")
2. One User (aliased "admin"), with organizationId set explicitly via `_ref`
3. One Member with organizationId and userId set explicitly via `_ref`

The SDK creates them in dependency order (Organization, then User, then Member) because the `_ref` edges say Member depends on both, and User depends on Organization.

### How does the SDK know the create order?

From the `_alias`/`_ref` graph in the payload — nothing else. It does NOT read your ORM's FK graph or relations. A record that another record `_ref`s is created first. A `_ref` to an alias that no record in the SAME payload declares fails with INVALID_BODY ("references unknown alias(es)").

You set every foreign key yourself, including the scope field. Use the exact FK column name from your schema -- whether you called it organizationId, orgId, tenant_fk, or anything else. The value is a `{ "_ref": "..." }` pointing at the parent's `_alias`. The factory for that model owns the actual write.

### Realistic example (org with apps, members)

  {
    "create": {
      "Organization": [{ "_alias": "org", "name": "Acme Corp", "slug": "acme-corp" }],

      "User": [
        { "_alias": "alice", "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@test.com", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } },
        { "_alias": "bob", "name": "Bob", "email": "bob@test.com", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } }
      ],

      "Member": [
        { "role": "owner", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" }, "userId": { "_ref": "alice" } },
        { "role": "admin", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" }, "userId": { "_ref": "bob" } }
      ],

      "Application": [
        {
          "_alias": "webApp",
          "name": "Marketing Website",
          "architecture": "WEB",
          "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" }
        },
        {
          "name": "Android App",
          "architecture": "ANDROID",
          "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" }
        }
      ]
    }
  }

## How the SDK orders records

The SDK has no relation introspection. It builds a dependency graph purely from the `_alias`/`_ref` edges in your payload and topologically sorts it: any record referenced by a `_ref` is created before the record that points at it. Key order in the JSON is irrelevant.

### Setting foreign keys

Every FK is your responsibility, expressed as `{ "_ref": "alias" }`. There is no "FK direction" distinction to reason about — every link, whether it points "up" or "across", is just a `_ref` from the record that holds the FK column to the record it depends on.

Examples:
- Application holds organizationId -> set `"organizationId": { "_ref": "org" }` on each Application record.
- Member holds userId and organizationId -> set both as `_ref`s on each Member record.

This is how you solve the "member-user distribution" problem -- give each User its own `_alias`, then point each Member's userId at the right one. Each member gets its own user, correctly wired.

## What to include in fields

Required: every field marked as required in your schema that does NOT have a default value, is not auto-generated, and is not an auto-updated timestamp.

Unique fields: must have unique values to avoid collisions when tests run in parallel.

  { "name": "Acme Corp", "slug": "acme-corp", "email": "admin@test.com" }

## What to omit

- id -- auto-generated by the database
- Fields with default values -- the database or ORM handles them
- Auto-updated timestamp fields -- handled by the ORM automatically

What you MUST include (the SDK does NOT fill these in):
- Every foreign key -- set it explicitly as `{ "_ref": "alias" }`. The SDK does not wire FKs for you.
- The scope field -- it is a FK like any other. Set it explicitly (usually `{ "_ref": "..." }` to the scope record). The SDK does NOT inject it.

Example: given a model with fields id (auto-generated), name (required), architecture (required enum), organizationId (FK + scope field), createdAt (default now), and updatedAt (auto-updated), you provide name, architecture, and organizationId:

  { "name": "My App", "architecture": "WEB", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } }

The SDK handles id, createdAt, and updatedAt. You set organizationId.

## Cross-model references (_alias / _ref)

Every foreign key is a cross-model reference: name the target record with _alias, and point the FK at it with _ref. This is the ONLY way to link records — there is no nesting.

### Example: TestGeneration needs applicationId

TestGeneration has an applicationId pointing at an Application, and Test has a testGenerationId pointing at a TestGeneration. Each model is a top-level key; the FKs are `_ref`s:

  {
    "create": {
      "Application": [{ "_alias": "webApp", "name": "Marketing Website", "architecture": "WEB", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } }],

      "TestPlan": [{ "_alias": "smoke", "name": "Smoke Plan", "plan": "content", "applicationId": { "_ref": "webApp" } }],

      "TestGeneration": [{ "_alias": "gen1", "conversation": "[]", "status": "success", "testPlanId": { "_ref": "smoke" }, "applicationId": { "_ref": "webApp" } }],

      "Test": [{ "name": "Homepage Test", "testGenerationId": { "_ref": "gen1" } }],

      "Step": [{ "order": 1, "interaction": "click", "params": {}, "testId": { "_ref": "homepageTest" } }]
    }
  }

Rules:
- _alias is a string name you choose. It must be unique across the entire payload.
- _ref resolves to the id of the aliased record after it's created.
- A _ref to an alias that no record in the SAME payload declares fails with INVALID_BODY ("references unknown alias(es)").
- Key order does not matter — the SDK topologically sorts records from the _alias/_ref graph, so a record is created before anything that _refs it.
- You can chain references: alias a record, then reference it from multiple places.

### Another example: Invitation with inviterId

  {
    "create": {
      "Organization": [{ "_alias": "org", "name": "Org", "slug": "org" }],
      "User": [{ "_alias": "inviter", "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@test.com", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } }],
      "Member": [{ "role": "owner", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" }, "userId": { "_ref": "inviter" } }],
      "Invitation": [
        { "email": "bob@test.com", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" }, "inviterId": { "_ref": "inviter" }, "role": "admin", "expiresAt": "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z" },
        { "email": "carol@test.com", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" }, "inviterId": { "_ref": "inviter" }, "role": "member", "expiresAt": "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z" }
      ]
    }
  }

### Another example: TestTag (join table)

  {
    "create": {
      "Tag": [
        { "_alias": "tag1", "name": "Critical", "color": "#FF0000", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } },
        { "_alias": "tag2", "name": "High", "color": "#FF8800", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } }
      ],
      "Test": [{ "_alias": "test1", "name": "Test", "testGenerationId": { "_ref": "gen1" } }],
      "TestTag": [
        { "testId": { "_ref": "test1" }, "tagId": { "_ref": "tag1" } },
        { "testId": { "_ref": "test1" }, "tagId": { "_ref": "tag2" } }
      ]
    }
  }

## The three standard scenarios

When writing scenarios for a project, create three:

### empty -- Org + user only
Tests empty states, onboarding flows, "no data yet" screens.

  {
    "create": {
      "Organization": [{ "_alias": "org", "name": "Empty Org", "slug": "empty-org" }],
      "User": [{ "_alias": "solo", "name": "Solo User", "email": "solo@test.com", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } }],
      "Member": [{ "role": "owner", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" }, "userId": { "_ref": "solo" } }]
    }
  }

### standard -- Realistic variety
Enough data to test every filter, status, and category. Use descriptive names ("Marketing Website", not "App 1"). Include at least one entity per enum value.

  {
    "create": {
      "Organization": [{ "_alias": "org", "name": "Acme Corp", "slug": "acme-corp" }],
      "User": [
        { "_alias": "alice", "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@test.com", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } },
        { "_alias": "bob", "name": "Bob", "email": "bob@test.com", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } },
        { "_alias": "carol", "name": "Carol", "email": "carol@test.com", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } }
      ],
      "Member": [
        { "role": "owner", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" }, "userId": { "_ref": "alice" } },
        { "role": "admin", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" }, "userId": { "_ref": "bob" } },
        { "role": "viewer", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" }, "userId": { "_ref": "carol" } }
      ],
      "Application": [
        { "_alias": "webApp", "name": "Marketing Website", "architecture": "WEB", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } },
        { "name": "Android App", "architecture": "ANDROID", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } },
        { "name": "iOS App", "architecture": "IOS", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } }
      ],
      "Tag": [
        { "name": "Critical", "color": "#DC2626", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } },
        { "name": "P1 - High", "color": "#F97316", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } },
        { "name": "Flaky", "color": "#EAB308", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } }
      ]
    }
  }

### large -- High volume
Exceeds pagination thresholds. Tests pagination, sort stability, filter performance. Each record is explicitly listed in the array.

  {
    "create": {
      "Organization": [{ "_alias": "org", "name": "Load Test Org", "slug": "load-test" }],
      "User": [{ "_alias": "user", "name": "User", "email": "load@test.com", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } }],
      "Member": [{ "role": "owner", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" }, "userId": { "_ref": "user" } }],
      "Application": [{ "_alias": "app", "name": "App", "architecture": "WEB", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } }],
      "Tag": [
        { "name": "Tag 1", "color": "#333", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } },
        { "name": "Tag 2", "color": "#333", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } },
        { "name": "Tag 3", "color": "#333", "organizationId": { "_ref": "org" } }
      ],
      "TestPlan": [{ "_alias": "plan", "name": "Plan", "plan": "x", "applicationId": { "_ref": "app" } }],
      "TestGeneration": [{ "_alias": "gen1", "conversation": "[]", "testPlanId": { "_ref": "plan" }, "applicationId": { "_ref": "app" } }],
      "Test": [{ "name": "Test", "testGenerationId": { "_ref": "gen1" } }]
    }
  }
